title: Throttled Promise Concurrency Pool
problemStatement: Implement `promisePool(taskFns, concurrencyLimit)` that takes an array of promise-returning functions and executes them with at most `concurrencyLimit` tasks running concurrently. Returns a Promise resolving to an array of results in the original order.
interviewTrap: Starting all promises simultaneously using `Promise.all(tasks.map(fn => fn()))` will overwhelm APIs or databases. Running workers that pull from a shared queue guarantees strict concurrency bounds.

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A Throttled Promise Concurrency Pool executes a collection of asynchronous task factories with a strict maximum concurrency limit `concurrency` (e.g. running at most 3 HTTP requests concurrently). As each task completes, the next queued task starts immediately.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Define an inner worker function that pulls the next task index from the shared cursor.
Execute task promise: `const p = Promise.resolve().then(() => taskFn())`.
Store the result in `results[currentIndex]` upon resolution.
When task finishes, remove its promise from the `executing` pool and trigger the next task from the queue.
Return the collected results array when all tasks have settled.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: Unbounded parallel execution (`Promise.all(10000Requests)`) exhausts operating system socket file descriptors, saturates network bandwidth, and triggers HTTP 429 / ENOTFOUND errors. A worker-pool architecture maintains constant memory and socket pressure.

complexity.time: O(T / concurrency) total wall-clock duration where T is aggregate task time.
complexity.space: O(C) active concurrency promise allocations in memory where C is concurrency limit.

edgeCasesHandled: Task list smaller than concurrency limit runs all tasks without deadlocking.

Tasks execute continuously without idle gaps between resolutions.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Why is running Promise.all on a large array (e.g. 5,000 requests) dangerous?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: Firing 5,000 requests concurrently exhausts operating system file descriptors / socket handles (`EMFILE` error), overwhelms DNS resolution, saturates network bandwidth, and triggers HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) or server crashes. A concurrency pool bounds active parallel work to a safe limit (e.g. 5 concurrent workers).
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Tests understanding of system-level resource constraints (sockets, memory, rate limits).

interviewCrossQuestions.question: How does a Worker Pool architecture maintain constant concurrency without idle gaps?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: Instead of chunking work into distinct batches of 5 (where worker 1 might finish in 10ms and sit idle waiting for worker 5 to finish in 1000ms), a true pool uses a shared task iterator cursor. The moment ANY worker finishes its current task, it immediately pulls the next available task from the queue, maintaining 100% worker saturation.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Distinguishes naive chunking (`Promise.all(batch)`) from true dynamic worker queues (`p-limit`).

interviewCrossQuestions.question: How should errors be handled in a concurrency pool?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: Two options depending on requirement: 1) Fast-fail: any error immediately rejects the outer promise and stops pulling new tasks from the queue. 2) Resilient: errors are caught, recorded as rejected outcomes, and remaining queued tasks continue executing.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Tests architectural flexibility in fault tolerance.

realWorldUseCases.description: Crawlers traverse sitemaps with strict limits (e.g. 4 concurrent requests per domain) to respect robots.txt and avoid IP banning.
realWorldUseCases.codeSnippet: const limit = pLimit(4); urls.map(url => limit(() => fetch(url)));

realWorldUseCases.scenario: Bulk Image Processing & Cloud Storage Uploads
realWorldUseCases.description: Processing 500 images via Sharp and uploading to S3: bounding concurrency to CPU core count prevents out-of-memory (OOM) crashes.

howToExplain.opening: A concurrency pool throttles asynchronous task execution to a fixed maximum window, maintaining constant throughput while protecting system memory and network sockets.
keyPoints: Unbounded concurrency triggers OS socket exhaustion and HTTP 429 rate limits.
Dynamic worker queues eliminate idle gaps by having workers pull the next item immediately upon completion.
Output array preserves original input index mapping regardless of task completion timing.
This is the production architecture implemented by libraries like p-limit and async.queue.
howToExplain.closingImpression: Concurrency limiting is the first line of defense against self-inflicted Denial of Service (DoS) in Node.js microservices.
analogies: A bank with 3 teller windows: customers wait in a single line, and the moment any teller is free, the next customer steps up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Chunking using `for (let i=0; i<arr.length; i+=limit)` with `Promise.all`.
commonMistakes.why: Chunking forces the entire batch to wait for the slowest task in that chunk before starting the next batch, wasting CPU time.
commonMistakes.correct: Use a shared index cursor where individual workers pull the next task immediately upon completion.

followUpDeepDive.question: How does Node.js libuv threadpool size affect asynchronous concurrency?
followUpDeepDive.answer: In Node.js, network I/O is handled non-blockingly by OS epoll/kqueue. However, file system operations (`fs`), DNS lookups, and crypto hashing are executed on libuv's internal C++ worker threadpool, which defaults to ONLY 4 threads (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=4`). Launching 100 concurrent `fs.readFile` calls will queue up on those 4 threads.
